local_facts.title: No new conventional septic tanks in Miami-Dade since 2023
local_facts.claim: On 7 July 2022 the Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners adopted Ordinance 22-83, which sorts septic systems into four tiers, from conventional Type 1 to performance-based Types 2, 3 and 4. Since 1 January 2023 a new system, or the replacement of an entire existing one, cannot be a Type 1, and homes within 1,000 feet of a surface water body need a Type 3 or 4. Every system in the county had to be registered with DERM by 1 January 2024.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Pumping, baffle and line repairs are routine. Replacing the whole system in North Miami is not: it now means an engineered, performance-based unit with a county plan review, which is why diagnosis comes before anyone quotes a new tank.

local_facts.title: About 9,000 county septic systems already sit too close to the water table
local_facts.claim: Miami-Dade County counts roughly 120,000 septic systems in use. Its Connect 2 Protect program says about 9,000 are vulnerable to compromise or failure from rising groundwater today, a figure projected to reach about 13,500 by 2040, and that South Florida groundwater sits just a few feet below the surface and usually peaks around September or October. The county's 2022 ordinance memo notes that a drainfield's bottom typically sits 6 to 24 inches above the Biscayne Aquifer.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A tank that copes in April can back up in October with no change in how the house uses water. Slow drains at the end of the rainy season are a groundwater problem as often as a full tank, and the fix differs.

local_facts.title: The 2020 fish kill ran from North Miami to Virginia Key
local_facts.claim: In mid-August 2020, dead fish, and stingrays and crabs crowding the shallows, were reported along Biscayne Bay from North Miami south to Virginia Key. State wildlife scientists attributed the kill to low dissolved oxygen tied to high water temperatures and heavy rain, with oxygen falling to zero in parts of the northern bay. Coverage at the time listed septic effluent among the nutrient pollutants that make such conditions worse.
local_facts.why_it_matters: North Miami drains to the northern bay, the stretch with the poorest circulation. A neglected tank or a drainfield sitting in groundwater is not only a yard problem here, which is why the county keeps tightening septic rules.

local_facts.title: Once sewer reaches the street, the clock is 365 days
local_facts.claim: Florida Statutes 381.00655 requires the owner of a working septic system to connect to an available public sewer within 365 days of written notice that service is available, or within 90 days of a health department notice if the system needs repair. The City of North Miami's own septic-to-sewer work has run in phases, 14 properties in phase 1 on $3.4 million in federal and state money and 47 properties in phase 2 on $600,000 in state funding.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A connection notice changes the job from pumping to abandonment. The tank has to be pumped out and properly abandoned under permit, and the timing of the last pump-out should match the sewer hookup.
